lessons.title: Parents & siblings
lessons.tip:
Two pairs for parents: **মা / বাবা** (*ma / baba*) are universal; **আম্মু / আব্বু** (*ammu / abbu*) are the warm, everyday words in many Bangladeshi (especially Muslim) homes — like 'mom' and 'dad'. In Kolkata and Hindu families you'll mostly hear মা and বাবা. Both pairs are correct: use whichever your family uses.

Siblings are simply **ভাই** (*bhai*, brother) and **বোন** (*bon*, sister). Remember: no word for 'is' and no 'a / the': **ও আমার ভাই** = 'He (is) my brother.'

Showing someone a photo? Start with **এটা আমার …** 'this is my …': **এটা আমার পরিবার** = 'This is my family.' (**পরিবার**, *poribar* = family.) Bangladeshi families are often large and close-knit, and grandparents, uncles and aunts may live under the same roof — which is why the next lessons have so many kinship words.

lessons.title: Elder & younger
lessons.goal: Distinguish elder and younger siblings; say his/her.
lessons.tip:
**বড়** (*boro*) = big, **ছোট** (*chhoto*) = small. With family they mean **elder** and **younger**: **বড় ভাই** = elder brother, **ছোট বোন** = younger sister. Bengali almost always says *which* sibling.

You don't call an elder sibling by name — that would feel cheeky. Instead say **ভাইয়া** (*bhaiya*, elder brother) and **আপু** (*apu*, elder sister). Younger siblings you *do* call by name. In Kolkata the words are **দাদা** and **দিদি** — but careful: in Bangladesh **দাদা** means *grandfather*, as you'll see next lesson.

Every pronoun has a 'my/your' form with **-র**: সে → **তার**, ও → **ওর**, উনি → **ওনার**, তুই → **তোর**. Like সে, they don't show gender: **তার নাম** = 'his name' or 'her name'. Use **ওনার** for someone you'd call আপনি, and **তোর** only with people you'd call তুই.

sentences.en: My elder brother is a doctor.
alt: My older brother is a doctor.
My big brother is a doctor.

sentences.en: My younger sister is a student.
alt: My little sister is a student.

lessons.title: Father's side
lessons.goal: Name grandparents, uncles and aunts on your father's side.
lessons.tip:
English has one 'uncle'; Bengali has a different word for each one! On your **father's side**:

- **দাদা / দাদি** — grandfather / grandmother
- **চাচা / চাচি** — father's brother / his wife
- **ফুফু / ফুফা** — father's sister / her husband (also said and spelled **ফুপু / ফুপা**)

To say 'father's', add **-র**: বাবা → **বাবার**. So **চাচা আমার বাবার ভাই** = 'Chacha is my father's brother.' Relatives are addressed by these words too: **চাচা, আপনি কেমন আছেন?**

**Watch out — Kolkata difference:** in Bangladesh **দাদা** is your *grandfather*, but in Kolkata (and many Hindu families in Bangladesh) দাদা means *elder brother*! There, paternal grandparents are ঠাকুরদা / ঠাকুমা, father's brother is কাকা, and father's sister is পিসি. This course uses the Bangladesh meaning: **দাদা = grandfather**.

sentences.en: My grandmother is a very good person.
alt: My grandma is a very good person.

lessons.title: Mother's side
lessons.goal: Name grandparents, uncles and aunts on your mother's side.
lessons.tip:
On your **mother's side**:

- **নানা / নানি** — grandfather / grandmother
- **মামা / মামি** — mother's brother / his wife
- **খালা / খালু** — mother's sister / her husband

Father's side or mother's side? Listen to the first sound: **দাদা / দাদি** (*da-*) are your father's parents, **নানা / নানি** (*na-*) your mother's.

'Mother's' is **মায়ের** (*mayer*). After most words ending in a vowel the possessive is just -র (বাবা → বাবার), but মা takes **-এর** with a little **য়** glide: মা → মায়ের.

**মামা** is a special word: in Bangladesh it's also how you cheerfully address a rickshaw driver or the man at the tea stall. You'll practise that in Lesson 6.

Kolkata: maternal grandparents are দাদু / দিদিমা, mother's sister is মাসি, her husband মেসো.

lessons.title: I have…
lessons.goal: Say what family you have and don't have; count people.
lessons.tip:
Bengali has no verb 'to have'. Instead you say **'to me there is'**: **আমার একটা বোন আছে** (*amar ekta bon achhe*) — literally 'My one sister exists' = 'I have a sister.' Note it's **আমার**, not আমি. The negative uses **নেই**: **আমার ভাই নেই** = 'I have no brother.' Question: **তোমার কি ভাই আছে?**

When you count, Bengali adds a **classifier** to the number. For people use **-জন** (*-jon*): **একজন** (one person), **দুইজন** (two people), **কয়জন?** (how many people?). In casual speech **-টা** is common too: **একটা বোন**.

Plural possessives: আমরা → **আমাদের** (our), তোমরা → **তোমাদের** (your, to two or more people you'd call তুমি). Others follow the same pattern: *apnader*, *oder*, *tader*.

Culture: 'How many brothers and sisters do you have?' is a perfectly normal first-meeting question in Bangladesh — as are questions about marriage and children. It's friendly interest, not nosiness.

sentences.en: How many children do you have?
alt: How many kids do you have?

sentences.en: How many children do you have?
alt: How many kids do you have?
How many children do you all have?

lessons.title: Calling strangers 'uncle'
lessons.goal: Address non-relatives respectfully with kin terms.
grammar: kin terms as polite address: ভাই, ভাইয়া, আপা, আপু, চাচা, খালা, মামা
survival chunks: আমি জানি না · বুঝতে পারছি না · আচ্ছা
lessons.tip:
In Bangladesh you rarely call an adult by their name or 'sir/madam'. Instead you **promote them into your family**:

- **ভাই / ভাইয়া** — any man around your age or a bit older (shopkeepers, waiters, colleagues)
- **আপা / আপু** — any woman a bit older than you
- **চাচা** — an older man; **খালা** — an older woman (also domestic helpers)
- **মামা** — rickshaw drivers, tea-stall owners, street vendors: friendly and informal
- **আংকেল / আন্টি** — friends' parents and older people in middle-class city life

These terms still take **আপনি** (polite verbs) unless you know the person well: *Chacha, apni kemon achhen?* — not *achho*.

Using them makes people warm to you instantly — a foreigner who says **মামা** to a rickshaw driver will usually get a big smile.

Three lifesavers for talking to strangers: **আমি জানি না** "I don't know", **বুঝতে পারছি না** "I don't understand", and **আচ্ছা** "OK / I see".

sentences.en: Brother, do you know where the doctor is?
alt: Excuse me, do you know where the doctor is?

lessons.title: Review: my family
lessons.goal: Describe your whole family, including spouse and children.
grammar: X মানে কী? 'what does X mean?'
lessons.tip:
Last new words: **স্বামী** (*shami*, husband) and **স্ত্রী** (*stri*, wife). In everyday speech many people say **বউ** (*bou*) for 'wife' — it also means 'bride'. (The ব in স্বামী is silent, which you'll learn about in the conjuncts script unit.)

Quick recap of the family map:

- **Father's side:** দাদা / দাদি (grandparents) · চাচা / চাচি (his brother and his wife) · ফুফু / ফুফা (his sister and her husband)
- **Mother's side:** নানা / নানি (grandparents) · মামা / মামি (her brother and his wife) · খালা / খালু (her sister and her husband)
- **ছেলে / মেয়ে** = son / daughter as well as boy / girl

One more reminder: in Bangladesh **দাদা** is your *grandfather*. If a friend from Kolkata says *dada*, they probably mean an elder brother.

To join two ideas with 'but', use **কিন্তু**: **আমার ভাই আছে, কিন্তু বোন নেই।** When you hear a word you don't know, ask **X মানে কী?** "What does X mean?". **সবাই কেমন আছে?** "How is everyone?" is the classic question about someone's family.
